Daniel’s core move—“real life as a proxy” early on, “numbers game” later—quietly treats *realism* as the key ingredient, but what actually does the work is closer to *coherence plus trustworthy feedback*. Players will happily use real‑world reasoning in worlds that are not realistic at all, as long as the game’s causal rules are stable and learnable through action: think of how players infer possibilities from consistent physics, legible affordances, and reliable consequences. In design terms, this is less “simulate reality” than “make the action space readable,” a point that echoes Don Norman’s emphasis on affordances and signifiers in everyday tools ([The Design of Everyday Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Design_of_Everyday_Things)). Cataclysm:DDA can skip tutorialization not merely because it’s realistic, but because it often lets players *test hypotheses* and see grounded outcomes; when that feedback loop breaks (missing mechanics, arbitrary abstractions), the “proxy” collapses into guesswork rather than immersion.

The second assumption is that *complexity* is what prevents the “equilibrium solved in your head” problem. Complexity can delay mastery, but it can also accelerate it if the system exposes dominant strategies or if players outsource the model to wikis/spreadsheets—at which point the “world model” becomes *more* explicit than in simple games. What seems more central to Daniel’s enjoyment is not complexity per se, but **strategic opacity produced by interacting systems whose local rules are intelligible while global outcomes remain hard to compress**—a dynamic studied in “complex systems” and emergence more broadly ([Complex system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_system)). That distinction matters because it suggests an alternative design target: not maximal complexity, but *anti-reductionism*—multiple viable paths, context-dependent payoffs, and enough uncertainty that optimization never fully dominates play.

Finally, the Stellaris example exposes a potential category slip: choosing civics “according to real-life beliefs” may be less “using reality as a proxy for the game’s model” and more “using the game as a canvas for identity expression.” That’s still meaningful, but it’s different: it relies on the game *accepting* moral/political role-play, not on the game *matching* real-world political dynamics. If Daniel means the stronger claim—that the game’s outcomes reward real-world governance intuitions—then the post would benefit from naming the fragility: players’ “real world” models vary wildly by culture, education, and ideology, so the same “proxy” heuristic can produce contradictory expectations. A tutorialless, realism-leaning design can therefore be immersive for one group and alienating for another, not because the system is wrong, but because “reality” is not a single shared reference model.
